facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
On 23 April 2012 five individuals (Mr I. Bakirov, Mr S. Davidis, Ms Y. Lukyanova, Ms N. Mityushkina and Mr S. Udaltsov) submitted notice of a public demonstration to the mayor of Moscow.

The aim of the demonstration was to protest against abuses and falsifications in the course of the elections to the State Duma and of the President of the Russian Federation, and to demand fair elections, respect for human rights, the rule of law and the international obligations of the Russian Federation.

On 3 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security approved the alternative route from Kaluzhskaya Square, down Bolshaya Yakimanka Street and Bolshaya Polyanka Street, followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
The march proceeded down Yakimanka Street peacefully and without disruption.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Bolotnaya Square at around 6 p.m. to take part in the meeting.
The applicant stood in front of the stage on Bolotnaya Embankment, within the area designated as the meeting venue.
According to the applicant, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. the area around him remained peaceful, although there was general confusion.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
The applicant was detained at the police station for at least thirty-six hours pending administrative proceedings.

In the administrative proceedings, the applicant was found guilty of failure to obey lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.

The applicant claimed that he had heard the police orders made through a megaphone to disperse, but in the general commotion he was unable to leave immediately and remained within the authorised meeting area until 7 p.m., when he was arbitrarily arrested by the police dispersing the demonstration.
The police apprehended the applicant and took him to a police van, where he waited for an hour before it left Bolotnaya Square for the police station.

The applicant was found guilty of disobeying lawful police orders and was sentenced under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation to fifteen days' administrative detention.

In the administrative proceedings, the applicant was found guilty of failure to obey lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant was charged with obstructing traffic and disobeying lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.

The Federal Law on assemblies, meetings, demonstrations, marches and pickets (no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004, the Public Events Act) required that notification of a public event be filed by its organiser in writing with the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities no earlier than fifteen days and no later than ten days prior to the scheduled date of the event.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of the officer's official duties relating to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the officer's performance of his or her official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 or by administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

Article 27.5 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences punishable, among other administrative sanctions, by administrative detention may be subject to administrative detention for up to forty-eight hours.

The security plan provided for security measures in Moscow city centre in view of the forthcoming authorised demonstration at Bolotnaya Square and anticipated attempts by other opposition groups to hold unauthorised public gatherings.

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. necessary measures were taken to push citizens away from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, Bolotnaya Embankment and Bolotnaya Street and to arrest those who resisted the most, during which twenty-eight police officers and military servicemen sustained injuries of various gravity, four of whom were hospitalised.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that the mass disorder organised by Mr S. Udaltsov and others led to the destabilisation of public order and peace in a public place during the conduct of a public event, put a large number of people in danger, and led to considerable psychological tension in the vicinity of Bolotnaya Square in Moscow, accompanied by violence against the police and the destruction of property.

According to the applicant, during the working meeting on 4 May 2012 the organisers and the authorities agreed that, since there was insufficient time for an on-the-spot reconnaissance, the assembly layout and the security arrangements would be identical to the previous public event organised by the same group of opposition activists on 4 February 2012.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 delineated the area allotted to the meeting, which included the park at Bolotnaya Square.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.

A cordon of riot police in full protection gear barred access to the park at Bolotnaya Square and continued along the whole perimeter of the meeting area, channelling the demonstration to Bolotnaya Embankment.
The cordon officers did not enter into any discussion with the protest leaders and no senior officer was delegated to negotiate.

During the period between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m., no senior police officers or municipal officials came to the site of the sit-down protest, and there was no direct communication between the authorities and the leaders of the sit-in.
The police cordon began to push the crowd into the restricted area and advanced by several metres, pressing it inwards.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.

The Expert Commission's report stated that from the moment difficulties first arose for demonstrators attempting to cross Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, demonstrators made repeated attempts to negotiate with the police over moving their cordons to allow protesters onto Bolotnaya Square.

The Expert Commission's report stated that in the two hours between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. there does not appear to have been any clear reason for the police decision to advance other than to divide the crowd up into smaller sections, and that there is little evidence that demonstrators initiated the violence.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at around 6.20 p.m. the police announced that the rally was cancelled and asked protesters to disperse, but the announcement was not loud enough to reach the majority of the crowd.

Ms N. Mirza testified that as she was later told by Police Colonel V. Biryukov, the protesters had sat down on the ground because the passage had been narrowed down, and she confirmed that the passage was much narrower than usual and there were metal detectors which were not supposed to be there.
Mr N. Svanidze testified that neither the Ombudsman nor anyone else was able to get the passage widened despite requesting it.

Mr Vasilyev testified that the Ombudsman told Police Colonel V. Biryukov to let the cordon be moved back so that people could pass, but Police Colonel V. Biryukov told him that it was outside his powers and that he did not know in whose powers it was, at which point the police began breaking the crowd up.

On the basis of the report written by Police Officer Y., the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka district established that at 8.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the applicant had been walking along the road at Bolotnaya Square and obstructing the traffic, and that he had then disobeyed lawful police orders to vacate the venue.
The Justice of the Peace rejected as unreliable two eyewitnesses' testimonies to the effect that the police had not given the applicant any orders or warnings before arresting him.

The applicant was found guilty of disobeying lawful police orders and was sentenced under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation to fifteen days' administrative detention.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if a standoff or other dispute arises during the course of an assembly, negotiation or mediated dialogue may be an appropriate means of trying to reach an acceptable resolution.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement agencies should be proactive in engaging with assembly organizers, that there should be a nominated point of contact within the law enforcement agency whom protesters can contact before or during an assembly, and that the policing operation should be characterized by a policy of 'no surprises'.
